summary: This Wikipedia-derived note surveys Tajikistan's demographics, history, economy and education. It covers the population and ethnic groups, ancient history from the Achaemenid Empire through the Silk Road and Kushan rule, and the spread of Islam. It also describes the economic role of labour-migrant remittances and the Soviet-era suppression of religion and the basmachi revolt.
one_line: Overview of Tajikistan covering its population, ancient and Silk Road history, remittance-driven economy, education system, and Soviet-era religious suppression.
key_facts: Tajikistan had a population of 7,349,145 according to a July 2009 estimate.
About 70% of Tajikistan's population is under the age of 30.
Tajiks who speak Tajik, a dialect of Persian, are the main ethnic group, with sizable Uzbek and Russian minorities.
The earliest recorded history of the region dates to about 500 BCE, when much of modern Tajikistan was part of the Achaemenid Empire.
Northern Tajikistan (Khujand and Panjakent) was part of Sogdia, overrun by Scythians and Yuezhi nomadic tribes around 150 BCE.
Chinese explorer Zhang Qian's expedition during the reign of Wudi (141–87 BCE) led to flourishing commercial relations between Han China and Sogdiana.
The Kushan Empire took control of the region in the first century CE and ruled until the 4th century CE.
Arabs brought Islam to the region in the early eighth century.
In 2010, remittances from Tajik labour migrants totaled an estimated $2.1 billion US dollars.
According to some estimates, about 20% of Tajikistan's population lives on less than US$1.25 per day.
The World Bank Tajikistan Policy Note 2006 concluded that remittances helped significantly reduce poverty.
Public education consists of 11 years of primary and secondary education, with a planned 12-year system in 2016.
As of 2008, tertiary education enrollment in Tajikistan was 17%, below the sub-regional average of 37%.
After the Russian Revolution of 1917, basmachi guerrillas fought Bolshevik armies in a futile attempt to maintain independence.
Soviet authorities discouraged and repressed Islam, Judaism and Christianity, closing many mosques, churches and synagogues.
